text: My grandmother kept a jar of bacon grease on the back of the stove for forty years. It sat in an old Maxwell House coffee can, and she'd add to it every Sunday morning without ceremony, a quiet inheritance from her own mother's kitchen. When she died, my aunts debated the house, the car, the silver — but nobody wanted the grease. I took it anyway. I don't cook with it. I'm not sure why I thought I needed it. It sits now on the back of my own stove, growing solid in winter and soft in summer, and sometimes when I can't sleep I come downstairs and stand in the dark kitchen and just look at it. There's something in its plainness that I find hard to name. It isn't grief exactly. It's more like proof — that she existed, that she stood exactly here, that the accumulation of ordinary mornings adds up to something worth preserving, even if you can't say what.

The river is three feet above flood stage and the color of coffee with too much cream. I'm standing on the bank watching a plastic lawn chair ride the current. Someone upstream lost their porch furniture. You can see, further out, the dark slick line where the main channel cuts — that's where the water is serious, where it would take you if you stepped wrong. There's a man next to me with his hands in his pockets who says, without looking at me, that this is nothing, that in eighty-seven it came up to the stop sign. He points to a green post forty feet behind us. We watch the chair until it rounds the bend. The sky is the pale yellow-gray that comes before more rain. Neither of us leaves. There's something about high water that makes strangers comfortable standing together in silence, something about watching a force that doesn't know your name.

I have changed my mind about ambition. When I was twenty-five I kept a list of things I intended to accomplish before I was forty, and the list was long and detailed and embarrassing in its confidence. Now I am forty-three and I understand that most of what I wanted, I wanted because I thought it would change how I felt inside, which was restless and vaguely insufficient. What actually changed the feeling, slowly, over years, was less dramatic: a friend who called without reason, work that required full attention, learning to cook three or four things properly. I'm not arguing against ambition. I'm arguing against the particular species of it that treats your own life as a problem to be solved, a deficit to correct. The list wasn't wrong about what I wanted. It was wrong about why I wanted it, and that error cost me most of my thirties.

She finds the letter on a Thursday in October, tucked into a library book she's had for six months, returned finally under pressure of guilt. The handwriting is her father's — unmistakably his, the F's too ornate, the numbers cramped. She does not open it in the library. She carries it home on the bus with it in her jacket pocket and her hand resting on it through the cloth. Her father has been dead for four years. She sits with the letter on the kitchen table for a long time. Outside, a kid on a skateboard goes past the window, then back the other direction, then past again. When she opens it, it is not what she expected — not wisdom, not apology, not a thing that resolves anything. It is a note reminding himself to buy more coffee filters. She laughs until she has to put her head down on the table. Then she smooths the paper flat and puts it in the drawer where she keeps things she can't throw away.

August is the month I trust least. It has the warmth of summer and the face of summer but underneath it is making preparations. You can feel it in the evenings — how the light shifts by eight o'clock, turning the quality of gold that belongs to something ending. The insects are louder than they were in June and somehow the volume reads as anxiety rather than vitality. I grew up in a climate with hard winters and I think that's why August registers as a kind of warning, a last-call feeling before something difficult. People who grew up in milder places don't understand this. They see a beautiful month and they're not wrong. But there are those of us who will always feel, in August's beauty, the particular pleasure of borrowed time — which is a real pleasure, fierce and specific, and nothing at all like peace.

The couple in 4B fights on a schedule I've learned to anticipate. Thursdays after nine, Sundays before noon. I don't know their names. I hear her voice more than his — sharper, higher, rising to a point. His is a low concession that sometimes becomes a wall. I have never once considered whether they are right for each other. That seems beside the point, maybe even a young person's question. What I think about instead, lying in my bed with one pillow pulled over my ear, is whether they know they're audible, and if so, whether they care, and what it means to care so much about something that you forget there are walls and other lives on the other side of them. There is something both terrible and admirable in it — to be that unguarded, that fully arrived in your own argument. I have been quieter than I should have been in most of my relationships and I'm not sure that was better.

We should talk about boredom more seriously than we do. Not the boredom of having nothing to do — that's easily solved — but the deeper kind, the kind that persists through activity, that arrives in the middle of parties, that sits at the back of your mind while you're doing exactly what you wanted to do. This boredom is a signal, I think, though I have not yet determined what it signals. Some people treat it as a failure of the self, something to medicate or schedule away. But I've come to believe it might be the psyche's honest report on the distance between your actual life and the one you're obscurely expecting. The tragedy is that we rarely stop long enough to ask what the boredom is pointing at. We reach instead for the phone, for noise, for the next thing. And the thing being pointed at recedes a little further. This seems like an important problem and we mostly treat it as a minor inconvenience.

The summer I was eleven we found a dog at the end of our road and kept it for three weeks before its owner came. The dog was old and smelled like creek water and we named it Captain. Three weeks is enough time for a dog to become yours, or for you to become the dog's, which is I suppose the more accurate direction of the transaction. When the owner came — a tired man in a truck who seemed relieved but not particularly moved — my brother and I stood in the driveway and watched without speaking. My mother had told us this might happen and we had said okay. Saying okay to something and being okay with it turn out to be different operations that nobody warns you about adequately. The dog looked back once from the truck bed. Or I remember it looking back. I was eleven and I needed it to look back, so perhaps it did, or perhaps I simply needed the story to go that way.

He takes the long way to work every day now, through the park, past the pond where the same two geese have apparently decided to spend the winter. It adds eleven minutes. His therapist, when he mentioned this, said that was good, that this was exactly the kind of thing she meant. He finds the geese surprisingly stabilizing — their complete indifference to him, their commitment to whatever geese are committed to, their willingness to stand in the cold at the edge of the water for no visible reason. There is a man who feeds them bread on Tuesdays and they seem no more grateful for that than for anything else. This feels instructive though he can't articulate the instruction. He is thirty-eight years old and has recently accepted that large parts of his emotional life will remain inarticulate, and that this is not the failure it seemed when he was younger. He watches the geese. They watch the water. This is enough.

It is possible to miss a place you never lived. I know this because I feel it about a town in the Scottish Highlands I visited for five days in my late twenties — a place where I knew no one, spoke to almost no one, walked every morning in cold that tasted like iron. I haven't been back. The five days were not particularly eventful. But I carry the place the way you carry a song that was playing during something important, even though the song had nothing to do with the thing. I think what I'm missing is not the place but the self I was while I was in it — briefly directionless, briefly emptied of obligation, briefly located in my body and in the weather with no requirement to produce anything at all. That self was temporary and I knew it. Missing it isn't grief. It's more like recognizing that you glimpsed something true and then had to get back on the plane.

My position on this is probably unpopular but I'll state it plainly: I do not believe most people who say they love mornings. What they love is the idea of themselves as morning people — the virtue of early rising, the extra hours, the moral architecture of it. I have tried mornings. I have set the alarm and padded to the kitchen in the dark and made the coffee and sat with it and felt almost nothing. The world at six a.m. does not speak to me. What speaks to me is eleven at night, when the obligations have wound down and the house is quiet and no one needs anything and I can read without guilt or think without interruption. I am not arguing this is better. I'm arguing it's honest, and that the cultural preference for mornings has made a lot of people — dutiful, committed, alarm-setting people — feel quietly inadequate for being most alive at the wrong hour.

The night before her wedding she can't sleep and goes to sit on the fire escape in her pajamas. The city is doing what the city always does, indifferent to the specificity of her situation. A taxi idles below. Someone two buildings over has a light on. She has no doubt about marrying him — this is what surprises her about her insomnia. She expected doubt and found instead something more like vertigo, the sensation of standing at a real threshold and being asked to step, not off a cliff, but off the known version of yourself into some adjacent future self who will be the same but different in ways she cannot preview. She has crossed thresholds before. They have all been fine. But this is the first one she chose completely, with no institutional logic or parental expectation doing any of the work. The taxi pulls away. She sits until she's cold, then goes back inside and sleeps immediately and dreams about nothing she can remember.

What I remember most about learning to drive is not the mechanics of it but the specific fear of my father in the passenger seat. He was not a man given to visible anxiety, but something about watching his daughter operate heavy machinery reduced him to a collection of tense silences and sharp inhalations at corners. He would brace one hand against the dashboard and say nothing. The saying nothing was worse than if he'd spoken. I have since driven hundreds of thousands of miles without incident. I have driven in cities that would have made that man in that passenger seat pray openly. But sometimes, backing out of a tight parking space, I can still feel the ghost of his hand bracing against nothing, his held breath, and I feel newly the pressure of being someone's whole concern concentrated in a moment, which was its own kind of love, anxious and specific and impossible to return directly.

In the town where my mother grew up there is a diner that has been there since 1958 and I don't think it has ever changed the menu. The laminated pages are yellow-brown at the edges. The booths are red vinyl repaired with strips of duct tape in two or three places that have become so familiar they've ceased to be repairs and are simply part of the booths now. The coffee is bad in a way that's almost historical — as if they decided in 1958 what coffee was and have been loyal to that decision ever since. My mother always orders the same thing. She doesn't look at the menu. She looks around at the other tables with a particular expression I can only describe as the face of someone reviewing evidence. She grew up in this town and left at eighteen and came back only for her mother's death and after that not often. But she always wants to eat here when we visit. I have learned not to ask why. Some places are not really about the food.

There are days when the bureaucracy of being alive feels particularly oppressive. The forms that must be filled, the passwords that must be reset, the hold music that plays its thirty-second loop while you wait to speak to someone who cannot actually solve the problem. I spent forty minutes on the phone last week trying to correct a billing error that the company acknowledged was their mistake. By the end I had been transferred twice and placed on hold three times and the error had not been corrected, and what I felt was not anger exactly but a kind of sedimentary exhaustion. This is I think one of the underacknowledged emotional textures of contemporary life — not suffering, nothing so clarifying as that, but the accumulation of low-grade friction that arrives in the form of forms and phone trees and impossible dropdown menus where your situation is never one of the listed options. It doesn't make for good tragedy. It makes for a tiredness that's hard to name at the end of a day that was technically fine.

She was the kind of teacher who remembered your name three years later in a grocery store, which sounds like a small thing until you remember being fourteen and invisible in the specific way that fourteen can make you feel. I wasn't a good student in her class. I sat in the back and drew in the margins of my notebook and contributed the minimum required to avoid consequence. She didn't seem to take it personally. She had this quality of finding something worth noticing in everyone, not in a performed way, not in the way that announces itself as kindness, but quietly, the way a good reader finds what a book is actually doing beneath what it seems to be doing. I don't remember what she taught. I remember that I felt, in her classroom, that I was being correctly seen — which is different from being praised, and rarer, and more sustaining. I think about her when I'm in a room and someone seems to be sitting in the back.

The tree came down in a storm and took half the fence with it. This was Tuesday. By Wednesday I had a chain saw in my hands for the first time in my life and was working through the larger branches with the careful focus of someone doing a physical task they don't entirely understand. There's a particular quality of attention that comes with dangerous equipment — a narrowing, a kind of forced presence that I don't arrive at easily in ordinary life. The smell of the wood was extraordinary. I don't know what kind of tree it was. I should probably know the trees in my own yard but I don't, and the tree didn't mind. By afternoon I had a pile of cut rounds and an aching back and a section of fence that needs replacing, and I felt more tired than I'd felt in months and also, unreasonably, better. Some physical objects want to be dealt with directly. There's a satisfaction in meeting them on those terms.

It's raining the afternoon they finally close the bookstore. He's watched it happen gradually — the reading series cancelled, the cafe removed, the children's section compressed to one shelf, then to a table, then gone. Today there's a sign in the window that's been there two weeks, which he read the first time but doesn't read again now. He just stands on the sidewalk in the rain looking at the window display, which someone has arranged one last time with some effort. There is something particular about losing a place where you used to be happy. Not a person, nothing so profound as a person, but a place with its own light and its particular smell and the knowledge of where things were. He's aware this is not the real tragedy of the year. The real tragedies were elsewhere and larger and happened to other people. But grief isn't ranked by scale when it arrives. It arrives at its own size and asks to be acknowledged, even when its size is one independent bookstore in the rain.

My son asked me last spring why we have to die and I said, honestly, that I don't know, and then I said some things about biology and about stars and about how nothing that works the same way forever stays interesting, and he listened politely in the way of a seven-year-old listening to an adult explain something they haven't asked about. Then he said, but why do we have to, and I understood then that he wasn't asking for information. He was asking me to object with him, to agree that this was not a good arrangement. I said, you're right, it isn't fair. He seemed satisfied with this and went back to what he was doing. I sat with it for the rest of the afternoon. There's a version of parenting that tries to resolve every hard question, to make the world legible and just. And then there's the other version, which is just sitting in the unfairness with your kid and being honest about it, which is harder, and which I think is more useful.

Friendship in middle age requires making arrangements. There are calendars to be consulted, distances to be driven, babysitters to be secured and dinner reservations and the whole logistical armature of people with too many obligations and not enough margin. I sometimes miss the days when seeing someone meant walking thirty feet down a dormitory hallway. And yet there is something in the arranged friendship, the one that costs something to show up for, that I've come to value in ways I couldn't have when everything was effortless. When my friend drives an hour and a half on a Friday night to sit at my kitchen table and drink wine and talk about nothing urgent, the act itself carries meaning that proximity alone couldn't supply. We chose this, against the friction. The friction is part of the message. I think what we're telling each other, every time we make the arrangements and keep them, is that we still regard each other as necessary. Which, past forty, is not nothing. It might be everything.
